title: Skates don’t melt ice by pressure: the textbook explanation fails
body: The classic explanation of slippery ice says a skate’s blade presses so hard that the ice beneath it melts into a lubricating film. In 1939 Frank Bowden and T. P. Hughes showed it can’t be the whole story: by that theory skating below about −4 °C would be impossible, yet ice hockey is played best at around −9 °C. Friction from the moving blade does generate heat, and a **liquid-like layer** of loosely bound molecules sits on ice even when nothing is pressing on it. Which effect matters most is still argued, with 2014 research pointing to frictional heating in most everyday conditions.

slides.heading: Three suspects
items: Pressure melting: real, but far too weak on its own
Frictional heating: the moving blade warms and melts a thin layer
A semi-liquid surface: molecules on top can’t bond properly to the ice below

slides.label: the optimum ice temperature for ice hockey
slides.text: Figure skaters prefer about −5.5 °C. Both are colder than pressure melting alone could explain.

slides.question: By pressure melting alone, skating would be impossible below what temperature?
slides.explanation: About −4 °C. Rinks are colder than that, so a blade’s pressure can’t be what melts the ice, as Frank Bowden and T. P. Hughes showed in 1939. Friction heat and a liquid-like surface layer matter more.

slides.heading: Still an open question
slides.text: Even standing still on ice can be slippery below freezing, which friction heating can’t explain, while microscope measurements have found surprisingly high friction on the surface layer. A full theory has to combine all three mechanisms, and the question is still an active area of research.

slides.question: What showed that pressure melting can’t be the whole story?
slides.explanation: By the pressure-melting theory, skating below about −4 °C would be impossible, yet hockey rinks are kept around −9 °C. Bowden and Hughes pointed this out in 1939.
